'''''Agave attenuata''''', commonly called the '''foxtail''' or '''lion's tail''' '''agave''' or the '''swan's neck agave''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Asparagaceae]] (the asparaguses, agaves and yuccas). Sometimes called the '''soft-leaf''' or '''soft-leaved agave''', the aforementioned animal-related names are a nod to the appearance of the plant's [[inflorescence]], which—after years, generally—rises slightly before gravity brings it back down, giving the bloom a curved, "swan"-like or "foxtail" look. The species' specific manner of flowering is unique in the genus ''[[Agave]]'' as most other species produce a towering, vertical display, reminiscent of a miniature tree.<ref>Robert Zander : Zander hand dictionary of plant names. Edited by Fritz Encke, Günther Buchheim, Siegmund Seybold. 15th edition, corrected reprint of the 14th edition. Eugen Ulmer, Stuttgart 1994, {{ISBN|3-8001-5072-7}}</ref>

In addition to its inflorescence, when compared with other ''Agave'' species, ''A. attenuata'' is further unique with its soft, spineless leaves and the fact that it does not rapidly [[Vegetative reproduction|asexually produce]] dozens of "runners" or "pups" from the [[rhizome]] of the mother plant. These factors have helped ''A. attenuata'' earn a positive reputation amongst gardeners as easy-to-manage; the species has become extremely popular as an ornamental plant in appropriate climates and zones, especially the [[Southwestern United States|American Southwest]], [[Latin America]] and the [[Mediterranean Basin|Mediterranean]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.cactus-art.biz/schede/AGAVE/Agave_attenuata/Agave_attenuata/Agave_attenuata.htm|title=Agave attenuata}}</ref>

Several unique forms and cultivars have been created and made available on the plant market, such as the white-[[Variegation|variegated]] ''A. attenuata'' 'Variegata' and 'Ray of Light', or the teal-hued 'Boutin Blue'. The similarly teal-leaved 'Blue Flame' was achieved with the cross of ''Agave attenuata'' x ''[[Agave shawii]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Agave Blue Flame — GDNC Nursery |url=https://www.gdncnursery.com/agave-blue-flame |quote=The hybrid was created in LA, California. Its parents, Agave shawii[,] is native to Southern California and Mexico's Baja California, which include[s] both desert and temperate coastal climate[s], and Agave attenuata[;] is native to central Mexico, which has warm and humid summers.}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Agave attenuata Pot 2250px.jpg|thumb|left]]
Although particularly young or smaller plants can appear [[Glossary of botanical terms|acaulescent]], stems often mature to between {{convert|50|and|150|cm|in|abbr=on}} in length, with older, desiccated leaves falling off and leaving the woody stems visible. The leaves are [[Leaf shape|ovate-acuminate]], {{convert|50|–|70|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|12|–|16|cm|in|abbr=on|0}} wide, pale in color, ranging from a light gray to a light yellowish-green. There are neither teeth, nor terminal spines, although the leaves taper to soft points that fray with age. The numerous, broad, succulent, tapering leaves are slightly less rigid than the leaves of most ''Agave'' species; they are a bright [[glaucous]] gray to light yellowish-green and stingless.<ref>Joachim Thiede: Agave chamelensis . In: Urs Eggli (ed.): Succulent lexicon. Monocotyledons (monocotyledons) . Eugen Ulmer, Stuttgart 2001, {{ISBN|3-8001-3662-7}} , P. 14-15 .</ref>

The inflorescence is a dense [[raceme]] {{convert|2.5|to|3|m|ft|sp=us}} high (usually curved), with greenish-yellow flowers, developing after many years.<ref name="gentry">[[Howard Scott Gentry]], ''Agaves of Continental North America'' (University of Arizona Press, 1982) pp. 66-71</ref> As with other ''Agave'' species, the species is [[monocarpic]], meaning that, rather than sending flowers out from the side of its stem and continuing living (like the succulent genera ''[[Crassula]]'' or ''[[Sedum]]'', for example), the entire rosette morphs into the giant [[inflorescence]]. After many months, this blossom subsequently dies following pollination and seed development, although numerous plantlets consequently sprout, both from the base of the plant and from the flower raceme. In nature, when the inflorescence finally dries and falls to the ground, the young plants growing from it will inevitably root into the ground, thus forming a brand-new colony.

It has two subspecies:
*''A. attenuata'' ssp. ''attenuata'': Native to Central and Southwest Mexico and naturalized in Madeira and Libya.<ref>{{cite web |title=Agave attenuata subsp. attenuata |url=https://www.catalogueoflife.org/data/taxon/5FFVZ |publisher=[[Catalogue of Life]] |access-date=18 January 2021}}</ref>
*''A. attenuata'' ssp. ''dentata'' <small>(J.Verschaff.) B.Ullrich</small>: Native to Northwest and Southwest Mexico.<ref>{{cite web |title=Agave attenuata subsp. dentata (J.Verschaff.) B.Ullrich |url=https://www.catalogueoflife.org/data/taxon/5FFW2 |publisher=[[Catalogue of Life]] |access-date=18 January 2021}}</ref>

==Etymology==
The Latin [[binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''attenuata'' means "with a narrow point".<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book | last=Harrison |first=Lorraine | title=RHS Latin for Gardeners | year=2012 |publisher=Mitchell Beazley | location=United Kingdom | isbn=978-1-84533-731-5 }}</ref>

==Range==
Specimens were sent to [[Kew Gardens]] by the explorer [[Henri Guillaume Galeotti|Galeotti]] in [[1834]] from an unspecified location in [[Mexican Plateau|central Mexico]]. A more recent study has reported it from [[Jalisco]], on the west coast and east of [[State of Mexico|Mexico State]], in small colonies at elevations between {{convert|1900|to|2500|m|ft|sp=us}}, but there have been few sightings, suggesting this species is rare in the wild.<ref name="gentry" /> [[International Union for Conservation of Nature|IUCN]] reports the species from the states of [[Colima]], [[Durango]], [[Guerrero]], [[Jalisco]], [[Michoacán]], [[Nayarit]] and Mexico State, at altitudes between {{convert|400|and|2500|m|ft|sp=us}} on volcanic rock cliffs within pine forests and transitional zones of [[tropical dry forest|tropical dry]] and [[temperate forest]]s types in mountains.<ref name="iucn status 20 November 2021" /> It is reportedly [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] in [[Libya]]<ref>[[Gordon Cheers]] (ed.): Botanica. Random House Australia 2003. German edition: Tandem Verlag GmbH 2003, {{ISBN|3-8331-1600-5}}</ref><ref name="CoL"/> and [[Madeira]]<ref name="CoL">{{cite web |title=Agave attenuata Salm-Dyck |url=https://www.catalogueoflife.org/data/taxon/5FFW2 |publisher=[[Catalogue of Life]] |access-date=18 January 2021}}</ref> and is widely spread through the [[Mediterranean Basin|Mediterranean]] and the rest of [[Macaronesia]].

==Cultivation==
[[File:Agave attenuata MHNT.BOT.2009.7.9.jpg|thumb|Dry seed capsules and seeds - [[MHNT]]]]
In cultivation, ''Agave attenuata'' is said to prefer relatively moist loamy soil, although it can cope with poor soil and dry conditions. It should be protected from direct sunlight in summer and from long periods of frost.<ref>[http://www.thelovelyplants.com/agave-attenuate-the-foxtail-plant/ Agave attenuata] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180919191757/http://www.thelovelyplants.com/agave-attenuata-the-foxtail-plant/ |date=2018-09-19 }}, The Lovely Plants</ref> It is hardy down to [[hardiness zone|USDA Zone]] 9b.<ref>{{cite web |title=Agave Species, Durango Soft Agave, Century Plant, Maguey |url=https://davesgarden.com/guides/pf/go/60644/ |publisher=davesgarden.com |access-date=18 January 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Agave attenuata (Fox Tail Agave) |date=29 April 2020 |url=https://worldofsucculents.com/agave-attenuata-fox-tail-agave/ |publisher=worldofsucculents.com |access-date=18 January 2021}}</ref>
